title: The Cyclospora Outbreak Was a Warning: Q&A with Saskia Popescu
gist: RAND epidemiologist Saskia Popescu says this summer's Cyclospora outbreak from tainted lettuce, which sickened thousands and killed two, exposes the U.S. food system as a critical but vulnerable soft underbelly. She argues the country underinvests in broad-spectrum biosurveillance, PPE manufacturing, and public trust, and flags AI as both a biosurveillance multiplier and a potential enabler of bioweapons and disinformation.

insights.claim: A Cyclospora outbreak linked to tainted lettuce sickened thousands and killed two people this summer, which a RAND biosecurity expert treats as a warning about broader U.S. vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Recurring food-borne outbreaks are a persistent tail risk for the fresh-produce supply chain and grocery/food-service names; traceability failures amplify recall scope and liability.
insights.quote: A parasitic infection linked to tainted lettuce has left thousands of people doubled over in pain this summer. Two people have died.

insights.claim: Biosecurity experts call the food system America's soft underbelly because it is so critical yet so vulnerable, and this outbreak highlights that fragility.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Frames food-supply resilience as a strategic-security category, not just a safety issue, pointing to policy and procurement demand for traceability and surveillance tech.
insights.quote: We call the food system America's soft underbelly, because it's so critical but so vulnerable.

insights.claim: Identifying an outbreak's source is inherently slow and difficult, requiring testing, tracing, and even calling people to ask what they ate weeks earlier across dozens of cases.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Slow source-identification prolongs recalls and market uncertainty; faster tracing tech (genomic, wastewater) is where investment reduces the damage window.
insights.quote: you're trying to identify likely sources and trends across dozens of cases, doing testing and tracing, even calling people and asking them what they ate weeks before

insights.claim: Popescu argues the U.S. focuses on a few big threats at the cost of others, when broad-spectrum investments like wastewater surveillance, PPE manufacturing, and cross-agency coordination would address the whole threat spectrum.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: A durable spending thesis: broad-spectrum biodefense infrastructure (surveillance, PPE) over single-threat programs, signaling demand for diagnostics and PPE capacity.
insights.quote: We focus everything on a few big threats at the cost of others.
insights.locator: What health threats most concern you

insights.claim: An outbreak response needs not just funding but cross-agency coordination, public support, effective communication, and people who can translate incoming information into action.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Coordination and communication gaps, not just budgets, are the failure points; institutional readiness is a non-capital constraint on response effectiveness.
insights.quote: You also need coordination across agencies, public support, and effective communication.

insights.claim: RAND recently published a report on strengthening U.S. PPE manufacturing capacity that highlights the role small- and medium-sized companies can play in making supply chains more robust.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Points to reshoring/scaling of domestic respiratory-PPE manufacturing among SMEs as a policy-backed opportunity after COVID-era shortages.
insights.quote: We just published a report on how to strengthen PPE manufacturing capacity in the United States
insights.locator: Beyond that, we could build up our supply chains

insights.claim: AI has significant potential to pull information from disparate networks and nodes to enhance biosurveillance capabilities.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: AI-driven biosurveillance is an emerging demand vector for public-health tech vendors integrating fragmented data streams.
insights.quote: It has so much potential to pull information from all the different networks and nodes and really enhance our biosurveillance capabilities.

insights.claim: Popescu warns AI could soon help someone develop a biological weapon or spread mis- and disinformation that hinders a critical response, making guardrails that do not block legitimate science a central open question at RAND.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Flags AI biosecurity risk as a live regulatory frontier; guardrail design will shape compliance burdens on AI and biotech firms.
insights.quote: there's also a possibility that it could soon help someone develop a biological weapon or spread mis- or disinformation that could hinder a critical response

themes.theme: Deterrence, trust, and the detection-response gap

insights.claim: Popescu recommends making the U.S. biosurveillance network robust against human, animal, and plant pathogens and being loud about it, so adversaries know testing U.S. biodefenses will fail and they will be caught.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Reframes biosurveillance as active deterrence, not just detection, linking it to national-security posture and adversary calculus.
insights.quote: We need our adversaries to know that they won't be successful if they test our biodefenses, and that they will be caught.

insights.claim: A recurring failure in outbreak response is a gap between detection and response, analogous to a fire alarm that only helps if you are home, hear it, understand it, and can call for help.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: The detection-to-action gap, not detection alone, is the bottleneck; investment in response translation and operations, not just sensors, is where readiness is won.
insights.quote: there's too often a gap between when reports start coming in and when an effective response gets underway

insights.claim: Popescu says the U.S. public is now less likely to follow public health guidance, and rebuilding trust in federal and state responses and in science is a necessary priority.
insights.speaker: Saskia Popescu
insights.so_what: Eroded public trust is itself a response-effectiveness risk; adversary-invested health disinformation campaigns compound outbreak severity regardless of medical capacity.
insights.quote: We have a public right now that is less likely to follow public health guidance, and we need to address that.
insights.locator: And then, we really need to rebuild public trust
